# CUDA

Two different pieces of software share the name "CUDA". Mixing them up is why `nvidia-smi` works but `nvcc` is missing, or why a wheel installs and then `torch.cuda.is_available()` is false.

**The driver** is the kernel module that talks to the GPU. If `nvidia-smi` prints a table of cards, the driver is fine. You need it on **every** machine that runs GPU code. It does not compile anything.

**nvcc** is the CUDA *compiler* (part of the CUDA toolkit). It turns `.cu` files into GPU binaries. You need it when you **build** an extension from source (a custom CUDA kernel, some robotics / rendering packages). You do **not** need it to *run* a PyTorch wheel: that wheel already contains compiled kernels and a matching CUDA runtime.

| You are… | Need driver? | Need nvcc? |
|---|---|---|
| Running `tensor.cuda()` / training with a PyTorch CUDA wheel | yes | no |
| `pip install` a package that compiles CUDA on this machine | yes | yes (toolkit compatible with that PyTorch) |
| CPU-only torch | no | no |

## Installing the driver and toolkit (Linux)

**1. NVIDIA driver (almost always first).** Install this on any machine that will run GPU code — including when you only use prebuilt PyTorch wheels. Without a loaded driver, `nvidia-smi` fails and `torch.cuda.is_available()` is false.

On Linux workstations, prefer the **`.run` installer** from [NVIDIA's driver download page](https://www.nvidia.com/Download/Find.aspx), not distro PPA packages mixed with leftovers from older installs. NVIDIA's [Omniverse Linux troubleshooting guide](https://docs.omniverse.nvidia.com/dev-guide/latest/linux-troubleshooting.html) walks through that approach: uninstall old drivers (`sudo nvidia-uninstall`), avoid (or purge) PPA-packaged `nvidia-*` if they left conflicting files, reboot, then run the downloaded `NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-*.run` (often from a TTY without the desktop session holding the GPU). Remote/headless boxes follow the same doc's notes on stopping the display manager before install.

That guide is aimed at Omniverse, but the driver steps apply to any CUDA stack (PyTorch, MuJoCo GPU, custom kernels). After install:

```bash
nvidia-smi   # should list GPUs; header "CUDA Version" is the driver's runtime cap
```

**2. CUDA toolkit / `nvcc` (only when you compile).** Skip this if you only `pip install` or `uv sync` prebuilt wheels. Install it when a dependency **builds** CUDA extensions on your machine (`pip install` hits `nvcc`, or you maintain `.cu` sources).

Options:

| Approach | When |
|---|---|
| [CUDA toolkit `.run`](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-downloads) or distro package | One system-wide toolkit version is enough |
| **`conda` / `mamba` env** (`cuda-nvcc`, `cuda-toolkit`, …) | Different projects need **different `nvcc` / toolkit versions** on the same box |

System-wide toolkit is fine for a single stack. **Conda shines when versions diverge:** PyTorch wheel built for CUDA 12.x, one research repo pinned to 11.8 for an old extension, another package's `setup.py` that insists on a specific `nvcc`. Create **separate envs** with the toolkit each build expects instead of fighting one global `/usr/local/cuda`. See [conda vs uv](environment-management.qmd#conda-vs-uv) — conda for the compiler/toolkit, `uv`/`pip` for Python packages inside that env still works.

Whichever path you use, the toolkit's `nvcc` version should be **compatible with your driver** (driver cap ≥ toolkit) and with the **CUDA tag** of the PyTorch (or other) runtime you run. Mismatch usually shows up at compile time (`unsupported GPU architecture`) or at import (`CUDA driver version is insufficient`).

```bash
which nvcc && nvcc --version   # optional — only after you install a toolkit
```

The driver advertises a **maximum** CUDA version it can run. The PyTorch wheel's tag (`cu128`, …) must not exceed that. `nvidia-smi` shows "CUDA Version" in the header — that is the driver's cap, not the toolkit you compiled with.

```bash
nvidia-smi
python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.cuda.is_available(), torch.cuda.device_count())"
```

Pick a GPU with [`CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`](environment-management.qmd#environment-variables). After that mask, this process's `cuda:0` is the first *visible* card, not necessarily physical 0.

PyTorch tensors live on a **device**. NumPy arrays do not. `x.cuda()` / `x.to("cuda")` copies; ops on `cuda` tensors run on the GPU. Mixing `cpu` and `cuda` in one expression is an error. Keep a batch on one device; `.cpu().numpy()` is a host copy (and a sync — [Bells and whistles](bells-and-whistles.qmd#bells-and-whistles)). See also [PyTorch CUDA semantics](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/cuda.html) and [References — GPU / CUDA](references.qmd#gpu--cuda).
